speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: WESTERN STOCK FEEDERS
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISPOSAL OF BEEF CATTLE AVAILABLE FOR MARKET
speechtext: I desire to direct two questions to the government through the Minister of Agriculture. Has the government carefully considered the seriousness of the possibility that undesirable prices and marketing conditions at present facing beef producers in western Canada may so discourage them as to cause an embarrassing beef shortage next year? Inasmuch as the present lack of markets confronting western Canadian producers might indicate that Canada does not need their beef, would the government consider permitting producers to sell their beef for a time in the United States market?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: WESTERN STOCK FEEDERS
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISPOSAL OF BEEF CATTLE AVAILABLE FOR MARKET
speechtext:
The question which has been raised by the hon. member for Lethbridge, on each of the last three sittings, I think, of the house, is answered in the following words:
During the first month of the present year, hog slaughterings have been at unprecedented levels and slaughterings of other classes of
Western Stock Feeders

live stock have been substantially greater than during the same period a year ago. Cattle slaughtered in Canada during the first four weeks of 1944 totalled 86,991 as compared with 52,279 during the same period of 1943, an increase of 34,712 head, or 66 per cent. Sheep and lamb slaughterings totalled 65,169 as compared with 44,318 in 1943, an increase of 20,851, or 47 per cent. Calf slaughterings were 24,795 as compared with 19,066, an increase of 5,629, or 30 per cent. Hog slaughterings totalled 901,767 as compared with 501,334 a year ago, an increase of 400,435, or 80 per cent.
I give these figures in order to call attention to the suggestion which is made in the question of the hon. member, namely that unless we do something now we are going to have a shortage a year hence, and to remind the house that I have heard that same story every year since the war began; and now this year, when we are entering upon the session, we are reporting an eighty per cent increase -in deliveries of, let us say, hogs, and comparable increases of other live stock coming in from the farms in different parts of Canada. The figures which I have given are only for the month of January, but comparable figures exist with regard to the three * months preceding the month of January, all of which should suggest to the house that there has' been very little in all this talk with regard to any possibility of there heir/; a decrease in meat supplies in Canada, at least in the immediate future. That, I would say, possibly would have some bearing even on the suggestion that there will be a decrease a year hence. Handling and movement of this record volume of live stock has taxed the capacity of the packing plants, storage warehouses and shipping facilities.
Purchases of bacon for the United Kingdom account have averaged over 20,000,000 pounds for several weeks, and an, average of 20,000,000 pounds for fifty weeks out of the year would be 1,000,000,000. I give these figures to emphasize the great quantities of live stock which are coming on the market at the present time.
All available storage space was used for storage, but all product over and above what could be stored was placed in cure for current shipment, and the record volume that had to be moved placed a great strain on- the shipping space available. I may say, with regard to this matter too, that recently three boats which were intended to be made available for the shipment of meat have met with mishaps, and that has made it impossible for them to take meat out until repairs are made. That too is a difficulty that governments cannot avoid during a war period,
[Mr. Gardiner.J
The following statement shows the storage stocks at January 1, 1944 as compared with January 1, 1943, the figures being in thousands of pounds:

000,000 pounds of export bacon stored for later shipment.
While at the moment, owing to heavy slaughterings of all classes of live stock during recent weeks, there is what might be considered a surplus of meat, the fact is that the United Kingdom desires all the surplus meat that Canada can provide. What happens to be a surplus at the moment is due to lack of shipping facilities to move the surplus product immediately. The reasons, in part, for that I have already given.
Steps are being taken to divert additional shipping space to Canadian ports not only for the purpose of handling additional 'bacon but also to lift surplus quantities of beef and mutton. That is a diversion of ships from some ports further south, to Canadian ports, in order to take out Canadian meat. That would emphasize the fact that there is just as great a difficulty in handling meat on the American side of the boundary line as there is on this side. As a matter of fact, there have been controls even more stringent with regard to getting hogs into packing plants on the American side of the boundary line than there have been on this side. All one needs to do at present is to examine the price levels in the two countries to realize that difficulties are as great on the other side as they are on this side.
Our pork to-day, in the markets in Canada, is bringing a higher price, with the premiums that are being paid, than the prices quoted on the American side of the line at the present time. This is particularly true of the Buffalo market as compared with the Toronto market. I have before me the figures on most live stock products. One would find it difficult to ship many live stock products into the United States under present conditions, pay the freight and any duty which there might be upon these meat products, and land the products in the markets there at higher prices than can be obtained here, or at prices as high as can be obtained in Canada, or at any rate as high returns as are here obtainable, including subsidies in some cases.
The immediate problem is (a) to secure additional shipping space and (b) to relieve the

Western Stock Feeders
congestion in cold storages by exporting products now in storage so as to permit the packing plants to handle and store the surplus live stock that is offered. The meat board stands prepared to purchase and export to the United Kingdom all surplus quantities of pork and beef, and arrangements are being made to export some quantities of mutton as soon as shipping space is available. Notwithstanding the heavy volume of live stock being offered- and this is important as an answer to a part of the question-prices for hogs and finished cattle have not been depressed, and all good butcher cattle has remained well above floor prices. With ample meat supplies available, the packers have found it difficult to move lower quality cattle and cows in the domestic market. The meat board found it difficult to handle the quantities being offered owing to the shortage of storage and shipping space, and in that connection I think I should say that there is no diffierence in the present conditions, so far as the marketing of live stock is concerned, as compared with conditions that always prevail. A man who is bound that he will ship live stock just when he thinks it ought to be shipped is always in the position, whether the government has control or has no control, of having to accept a price lower than the market would have provided for him had he waited another week or two to deliver. In the present situation, under more or less government control, he can move his live stock, more particularly cows, and have those cows processed in packing plants, frozen if necessary in the form of beef, and shipped to Britain. That is the market which is available under the arrangements now made, and when the government says to people with cows, "You had better hold them off for another two or three weeks, or another month, if you want to get a fair price for them," I submit the hardship is no greater in doing that than it was when on other occasions one was obliged to do it in order to meet the laws of supply and demand. That is the situation which does exist at present and it is creating some difficulty.
There is one other thing I hesitate to say, but I ought to say it in view of some of the representations that have been made in the resolutions which are coming to us from the section most affected, and that is that cows that run on the range have to be marketed somewhat earlier in the season than many cows that do not run on the range. The reason for that is obvious to men who are accustomed to handling cattle in the range country. It is that the cattle have to be got to the butcher before calving time comes. I am not so sure that getting them to the bqtcher before that
time will affect the quantity of meat in the manner suggested a few moments ago. It might even increase the quantity to have the cattle kept off the market. That may not meet the wishes of those desirious of selling cattle at present, though it does affect somewhat the price that can be secured for the quality of beef obtainable from a cow that is heavily in calf. While an ample meat supply is available, the packers have found it difficult to handle the lower quality cattle and cows in the domestic market. The meat board found it difficult to handle the quantities offered owing to the shortage of storage and shipping space. During the past few days, however, the board has been able to accept immediate shipment of some seven million pounds of beef, and this movement has had an immediate effect on cow prices, which moved sharply upwards in all markets. There is every reason to believe that in future all surplus beef available will be handled and lifted as offered for export. There has been a decline in sheep and lamb prices as a result of the temporary over-all meat position. While there is no floor price established for mutton and lamb, steps have been taken to export some of the surplus accumulation now in storage with a view to creating a better market for this class of live stock.
That, I think, covers the position pretty well with regard to the matter of beef, particularly the lower qualities which are not required on our home market. There does not appear to be any difficulty in connection with the quality of beef which is required on the home market.

['Doctor Collins, who
practised in Hudson Bay Junction at that 
time. By and by we did have a change of government. Under that Liberal administration we did get much better treatment.- We were without a doctor for some considerable time, as no doctor could provide medical service for this large area under such conditions. There was not a doctor within seventy miles when he left for another location. His going was a great loss to our community.
How would hon. members like to live in a community where there was no doctor within seventy miles to look after people who became sick. But when the Liberal government did decide to do something about those people, they madte provision for $50 a month to pay the doctor. The doctor had to agree that every person who was on relief could come to him and receive treatment. He was not prevented from making additional collections. But people who were getting $10 a month for relief, and were selling cordwood at a dollar a cord were not likely to be able to pay much to a medical doctor. However, the doctor was concerned about the health of the people, and he did accept $50 a month from the provincial government, and did give medical service to the people in a very large area.
I submit that $50 a month to give comprehensive service to such a large number of people in an area where the nearest hospital and doctor is seventy miles away is not sufficient. Many of the people in that area were men who had fought for their king and country at the time of the last war. That was one of the areas which was available for settlement when they came back from overseas. They settled on these bush homesteads, up in the north country.
After criticizing ourselves for our failure to care for people in times of sickness, we might ask ourselves if people in other countries have done better. If we examine the evidence placed before us in this large volume by the advisory committee I think we shall find that there are two countries which have outstanding records, as far as providing health for their citizens is concerned. I refer to New Zealand and Russia. And, in passing, I urge hon. members to take advantage of the opportunity to hear Doctor Sigerist this evening in the Glebe collegiate, or to-morrow before he leaves the city. Hear what this outstanding professor of the history of medicine has to say about what has been done in Russia.
In his book, which I have before me, I find
some significant statements. He says this:
It seems to me that the following four points represent the mdst characteristic features of the soviet health system:
1.	Medical service is free and therefore available to all;

The Address-Mr. Nicholson
2.	The prevention of disease is in the foreground of all health activities;
3.	All health activities are directed by central bodies, the people's commissariats of health, with the result that-
4.	Health can be planned on a large scale.
Then he says:
There can be no doubt that the soviet system of social insurance is infinitely superior to any insurance system in capitalist countries. The costs are what they should be, part of the cost of production. The benefits are infinitely greater than under any other insurance scheme. The worker is guaranteed complete medical service, he is given social security. He is entitled to it, because after all, he is creating the values that make such a scheme possible.
Most people are agreed that changes will have to be made in our health programme in Canada. Some doubts exist as to what type of changes should be made. I have here a copy of "You Knew What You Were Voting For", written by William S. Gibson, President of National Cellulose of Canada, Limited.
On page eight he says:
All the planners start with the premise- "We must not have another depression." I could bring many arguments to show that nations and individuals profit more in adversity than in good times. I know that I would rather start a new enterprise during a depression than in good times.
Of course Mr. Gibson would rather start an enterprise in poor times. In January I talked to a man working in one of the sawmills in my riding. He is receiving forty cents an hour and his board, but he told me that the first time he met me, in 1932 or 1933, he was working for four cents an hour for a ten-hour day. They could not even make it five cents an hour. Naturally Mr. Gibson would rather start an industry when he could have his materials produced by men working in the bush for four cents an hour, when there are fifty men looking for every job available.
I think this war has proven one thing conclusively. It has proven that if we want it we can have a high standard of living in Canada in the world of to-morrow. We should understand that a nation can plan its production and consumption on a low plane, with mass unemployment and low standards, or on a high plane with full employment and high standards for its people. I should like to point out that it was stated by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), when he was Minister of Finance, that whatever is physically possible must be made financially possible. His successor, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), has emphasized that. We must always keep that in mind. If that is true in war time, then it is equally true in peace time. Whatever is physically possible in peace time must be financially possible.
I have not the time to go into all the details that must be considered, but finance is not now and should not be a limiting factor in our effort in any direction. The only limiting factors should be: first, raw materials; second, labour; third, the machinery of pn>
duction and, fourth, our power to coordinate these things. I submit that if the war should end to-morrow-we know that victory will be achieved some day-Canada would be a richer nation than ever before. By that I mean that we would have more new factories, more trained workers and more new resources to develop.
In order to plan a health programme for the post-war period there are certain physical necessities which must be kept in mind. We must have: first, nutritious food; second, adequate supplies of heat, light, potable water, sewage disposal facilities and fresh air; third, preventive and restrictive health services; fourth, adequate clothing and proper housing for all our citizens. I shall have something to say about most of these at some future time.
Mention was made a few days ago by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) of an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal and which had been prompted by the report of a speech by Mr. Jolliffe, leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Ontario. During a discussion before a group of eminent medical men Mr. Jolliffe outlined in some detail the plans of the C.C.F. for improved medical services. This was during a meeting of the London academy of medicine on September 23, 1943. In his remarks Mr. Jolliffe made it quite clear that on the whole the doctors of this country had done a good job. We do not want to place the doctors of Canada in a position where they are not going to have a great deal of freedom. The president of the Canadian medical association made some reference to the fact that the C.CE. would limit the salaries of general practitioners to $3,000, and of specialists to $8,000. I have made a careful survey and I can find no record anywhere where any C.C.F. speaker made any statement of that kind.
I would remind the house that in Russia they have provided the highest standard of living available for their doctors. The C.C.F. in any province in Canada would recognize that our doctors are highly trained and must be given as high a standard of living as we can provide collectively.
Then the hon. member for Peterborough West asked if the C.C.F. could arrange for babies to be delivered between eight a.m. and five p.m., but no answer was given. Both the editorial in the Journal and the hon. member for Peterborough West assume that', 'Post-War Reconstruction
no answer could be given. Again I would remind the house that arrangements have been made to look after the medical and dental needs of our troops without any one doctor having to work for twenty-four hours a day.
Some of my best friends are of the medical profession and I have the greatest respect for them, but there is one thing I must say about them. While they are ready to look after their friends, most of them seem to be unable to look after themselves. Many of them are burnt out by the time they reach fifty or fifty-five years. We must provide machinery so that the medical services of this country can be carried on without any one doctor having to work for sixteen or twenty hours a day.

The hon. gentleman has quoted May, at page 173, and that dictum of May has been adopted by Doctor Beauchesne in his latest book, of which all hon. members have copies; it appears in citation 336 at page 135. I would draw to the attention of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken citation 335 on the same page:
A motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words; (b) by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
The subamendment now before the house seeks to add other words to the original amendment. Then citation 338, at page 136 of Beauchesne, reads:
The object of an amendment may be to effect such an alteration in a question as will obtain the support of those who, without such 100-20
alteration, must either vote against it or abstain from voting thereon, or to present to the house an alternative proposition either wholly or partially opposed to the original question. This may be effected by moving to omit all the words of the question after the first word "that", and to substitute in their place other words of a different import. In that case the debate that follows is not restricted to the amendment, but includes the motives of the amendment and of the motion, both matters being under the consideration of the house as alternative propositions.
As the hon. member has pointed out, under citation 367 at page 142, great latitude is allowed in the debate on the address, and exceptions taken of a highly technical nature as a rule are not considered when amendments are made in that debate. The effect of the amendments is as follows. The motion is made; the amendment is moved, and the subamendment follows. In our practice the procedure is to deal first with the subamendment; then .having disposed of that either by adoption or rejection, we deal with the amendment. If the subamendment is approved, then the amendment is put before the house as amended by the subamendment; and in like form when dealing with the motion, if the amendment has been adopted, then the motion is placed before the house as amended by the amendment or the subamendment as the case may be. The consequence is that in the debate which is taking place hon. members are addressing themselves to the motives contained in the original motion, the amendment and the subamendment, and additions to an amendment, when adopted, are really additions to the main motion.
For the reasons I have stated I think this subamendment is in order. The hon. member who raised the point of order referred to the question of relevancy. If one is dealing with all the motives contained in either the motion, the amendment or the subamendment, then the question of relevancy has some bearing, not as directly affecting the amendment or subamendment but as affecting the subject matters of the three motions before the house. In this case we are dealing with the speech from the throne, which embodies many principles; and the principles which have been set forth in the subamendment of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) are I think relevant to the subject under discussion. For that reason I am of opinion that the subamendment moved by the hon. member is in order.

Mr. Speaker, with one statement that was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the course of his remarks the other day I am in complete accord; that was when he said, as reported at page 34 of Hansard:

298	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
... I am opposed to parliaments extending their own terms of office. I think one of the greatest mistakes made in this country was the extension by one parliament of its own term of office.
With this point of view I am in complete agreement, as I ' think most people will be who are desirous of retaining our free institutions and maintaining our democratic form of government. It is a great pity, however, that the Prime Minister was not able to impress his point of view upon the Liberal government of Saskatchewan, which last April supported a bill to extend its own term of office. This was done in spite of the protests of the official opposition. What has amazed most people has been the complete acquiescence of the federal government in this very apparent violation of established constitutional procedure. I have made a careful search of the records, and I cannot find a single case in the history of the parliament at Westminster, or of any of the self-governing dominions, or of any of the legislatures of the Dominion of Canada, in which a parliament or a legislature extended its own term of office without the consent of the official opposition.

speechtext:
If the Prime Minister will have patience with me I shall some to that very point, as to what I think the government ought to have done. In 1916 Sir Robert Borden introduced a humble petition asking the parliament of Westminster to amend the British North America Act to extend the life of the Canadian parliament. On February 8 of that year, as reported at page 622 of Hansard, he said:
It is hardly necessary to say that it is a motion which we should not press if hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house should oppose it as a party. In that case 1 should feel it to be my duty to withdraw the motion, and then it would naturally be for the government to consider its course.
He was followed in that debate by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who at page 634 of Hansard is reported as having said:
If this resolution was not adopted unanimously, even though carried by a majority of this house, and even if my right hon. friend himself were to carry it to the foot of the throne, I have no doubt whatever that in the face of such a minority as would be arrayed against it, the British parliament would never grant the power sought.
A similar petition was introduced in the following year by Sir Robert Borden, but when some of the official opposition expressed

their disapproval the Prime Minister immediately withdrew the resolution on the ground that unless the opposition gave virtually unanimous consent the British parliament would be unwilling to permit the Canadian parliament to extend its own life. It has remained for a Liberal government in Saskatchewan to defy the parliamentary traditions of several centuries and use its majority in the legislature in order to cling to office without giving the electorate an opportunity to express their wish in the matter.
The Prime Minister asks what we think the federal government should have done about it. May I point out that the federal government, and particularly the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), have a responsibility to discharge to the people of Canada, and especially to the people of Saskatchewan. Under the British North America Act the power of disallowance was given to the federal government not merely to prevent the passage of legislation which might be considered ultra vires; as a matter of fact legislation of that kind can be taken care of very well in the courts. The power of disallowance was granted to the governor in council, in order that, as George Brown put it very succinctly:
... no injustice shall be done without appeal in local legislation.
The Minister of Justice is charged with the responsibility of seeing that provincial legislatures cannot pass legislation which deprives Canadian citizens of their democratic rights. The Minister of Justice and the government have been quick to use this power of disallowance when property rights were at stake, or when Canadian bankers felt that they were being discriminated against. But when the people of Saskatchewan were being denied the right to decide who would constitute the government of that province the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister failed to take any action. It is not enough for the Prime Minister to say that he is opposed to parliaments extending their own terms of office. He must do more than that. He must act. He is the custodian of the rights and privileges of the Canadian people, and in failing to disallow legislation by which the Saskatchewan government extended its own life the Prime Minister and his government, it seems to me, were derelict and negligent in the discharge of their duty.

speechtext:
May I say
to the Prime Minister that the only reason why I am at the present time an absentee leader in Saskatchewan is that the Liberal government of Saskatchewan has not dared to call any of the four by-elections that are due, or a general election in that province.
May I now turn to the speech from the throne-and I hope I shall be given some extra time, because of the interruptions made during my speech. This is the ninth debate on speeches from the throne I have witnessed in the house, and I must say it is the most astounding of them all. A speech from the throne debate is not generally considered something to be got rid of. It has generally been considered a debate during which several ministers of the crown would give an account of their stewardship, and during which they could outline the legislation they intend to present to the house. It has been considered that during the debate on the speech from the throne ministers would enunciate the principles and directives underlying that legislation. This debate would probably have closed last night, had it not been for the subamendment, and yet not a single minister on the treasury benches has taken part in it, with the exception of the Prime Minister-and he did not discuss the speech from the throne, but rather discussed Mr. John Bracken, and the speeches made by Lord Halifax and General Smuts.
Why this veil of silence? The ministers of the government make me think that the government programme is something like a little boy who has been given a lovely Christmas box wrapped in silver paper and bound with red ribbon, and that they are now standing aside in apprehensive timidity lest the little boy should ask permission to open it in order to see what is inside. I do not think they care to discuss this very promising programme they have placed before the Canadian people. After all, it is not sufficient to say that the war appropriation resolution will serve as a substitute. The people of Canada would like to know what plans the government have to deal with that period of transition from a war-time to a peace-time economy. That will not be covered by the war appropriation measure. Has the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) no plans concerning the period of transition to place before the house? Has the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) nothing to say about the tremendous problems
300	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
which will face agriculture when some of these subsidies are withdrawn, and when agriculture is faced with peace-time problems? Yet none of these ministers has had a word to say in the course of the debate.
In some quarters, this speech from the throne has been held out as an epic-making document, while in others, the people are suspicious of it, and it is not hard to understand why they are suspicious. I hold in my hand two documents, the first of which is a copy of a paper dated August 13,	1919, containing the
programme passed at a Liberal convention at which the present Prime Minister was elected as leader of the Liberal party. It certainly is a promising document. I see here that the principal articles of food are to be placed on the free list. Farm implements, farm machinery, flour mill and saw mill machinery and repair parts are to be placed on the free list, and wearing apparel and footwear are to have a reduction of at least fifty per cent in duty. I see further that there is to be an increase in the British preference to fifty per cent. I see further a resolution moved by W. L. Mackenzie King and seconded by Arthur Roebuck-a most interesting resolution. I cannot read it all, but I notice that they were to give us the federal incorporation of cooperative associations. I notice further tha,t there was to be an acceptance of the principle of proportional representation. Then I find here a long resolution moved, I believe, by Colonel Ralston, who is now Minister of National Defence; and it is just as rosy as some of the promises which now, twenty-five years later, appear in the speech from the throne. Soldiers were to have cash grants, such grants to be in addition to the present gratuity and pay for disability resulting from service. It states:
That such pensions or allowances be granted as shall enable soldiers or their dependents, as the ease may be, to maintain a liberal standard of living sufficient to guarantee health, education and all the necessities, comforts and amenities which go to make up a standard of living worthy of Canadian citizenship.
After twenty-five years each of those promises has been more honoured in the breach than in the observance. I have another document here which helps to make me more sceptical about the speech from the throne. This is a reprint of the statement handed to the press by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the night of the general election, October 14, 1905. It is an interesting document. It states:
The election is an endorsation of the Liberal view that credit is a public matter, not of interest to bankers only, but of direct concern to every citizen.

*Audi again:
The electorate has declared that a responsible ministry, not organized finance and international money power, is to control in all matters of state.
It says:
It is a verdict for the democratization of industry, in the rights of labour and consumers to have their voice heard and influence felt in the control of industrial policy. It is a warning and rebuke to arrogant employers of labour who have sought to intimidate their employees to prevent them from enjoying the free exercise of the franchise which is the birthright of every Canadian citizen.
I ask hon. members to put that statement alongside P.C. 9384 and see how they compare. Further on in the same statement:
It is a verdict in favour of personal liberty, electoral reform, and of measures which will, among other things, prevent the national radio being surreptitiously used by any political party for the defamation of character.
And again:
It is a verdict in favour of a more equitable distribution of wealth, with increasing regard to human need, to the furtherance of social justice, and to the promotion of the common good.
Then one more statement:
In the new era which dawns to-day. the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and misery, are the enemies w-hich Liberalism will seek to banish from the land.
Andl again:
We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty, starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance, discontent and distress in a country more blessed by Providence than any other on the face of the globe.
This effusion of eloquence was followed by four years of young men riding the rods, with 400,000 unemployed and in the neighbourhood of a million people on relief. Is it any wonder that we are rather sceptical of the speech from the throne and the fine promises that are now held out to the Canadian people? As a matter of fact, when one comes to examine the promises they are not so specific. After a cursory mention of the fact that the first objective must be the winning of the war, the speech from the throne proceeds to say that there are three main tasks which must be accomplished after the war: first, demobilization; second, conversion of our machinery of production from a war-time to a peace-time economy, and, third, social security measures.
With regard to demobilization it says that a broad programme has already been developed. Are we to take from this that the

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
machinery now set up for the demobilization, and care of our discharged men is the ultimate? Has the government nothing new to add except establishing a veterans' welfare department? Is there no new machinery to be added? If there is not, then heaven help the thousands of young men who will be coming back after this war. Heaven help them if something more adequate is not provided by the government. ,
With regard to the transfer from war-time to peace-time economy the speech from the throne states that the maintenance of full employment will "require" certain things. There is no statement as to how it is proposed to accomplish them. Two things are mentioned, an industrial bank and a sop which is thrown out to industrialists in the form of certain tax modifications.
Then we come to number three, social security. Some newspapers have set out fourteen points covering what the government is going to do, but the speech from the throne does not say what the government is going to do. The social security measures that have been set up already are very meagre, and the speech states-that the working out of a comprehensive national scheme will require further consultation. Then follows the only promise:
My ministers will welcome opportunities for such consultation.
That can mean very little, "will welcome opportunities for further consultation." It states further that they are prepared to provide for federal assistance in a nation-wide system of health insurance. There is no guarantee there that they are going to set up a nation-wide system of insurance. It states only that they are prepared to provide assistance. Anyone who has examined the findings of the Sirois report knows perfectly well that the provincial governments with their present limited sources of revenue will require more than assistance; they will require that the federal government either accept almost full responsibility or give to the provincial governments much larger sources of revenue than are now available to them.
In the light of what has happened in the past; in the light of these very vague statements, we in this group are not greatly encouraged by the speech from the throne. We shall welcome any social security measures which the government may bring down during this session, but we have no confidence as yet that these measures will be adequate or that the government is prepared to deal with the fundamental economic base which must be set up in order to provide full employment and make possible adequate social security.
May I deal now with what the speech from the throne says about agriculture? In all of the long speech-this is one of the longest for many years-only three lines are devoted to agriculture. It states:
To ensure economic stability for agriculture, you will be asked to make provision for a price floor for staple farm products.
That will all depend upon what the floor is. If it is a basement floor it will be of no value. If it is to be the floor we now have it will be of little worth the moment subsidies now paid under the War Measures Act are taken away.
I may say to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the farmers of this country are concerned as to what will happen when the subsidies now being paid-subsidies which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has suggested are being paid for the benefit of the consumer and not for the benefit of the producer-are removed. The floors which are now set will be totally inadequate.
It is true that the farmer has been receiving better prices for some of his products durmg the past few months. This may be partly due to the fact that two by-elections in western Canada did not deal very kindly with the Liberal candidates and it may be due partly to the fact that we are coming close to a federal election. As a matter of fact, I have always suspected that if you X-rayed a Canadian farmer you would find that he was pretty well streaked. There would be four streaks of lean for the four hard years and then one streak of fat for the election year. Every four or five years something has to be done for the farmer, and then he goes back to the lean years again after the election year.
The case of wheat is a good example. For years, hon. members on this side of the house have asked the government to suspend trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange and to establish a parity price for wheat. A delegation of four hundred farmers came here from Saskatchewan nearly two years ago and placed their case before the cabinet. No action was taken. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and I both moved motions last year in this house calling upon the government to take steps along the lines I have already mentioned. No action was taken. But this past year, when the world surplus of wheat was shrinking visibly and the demand for wheat was causing the price on the open market to rise, on the 28th of September the government stepped1 fn, suspended trading in wheat, and fixed the price at 81.25; and fourteen days later, on the 12th October, passed an order in council giving them authority to do what they had done fourteen days before. Why? Because as a matter of fact the government, which had
302	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
pinned its faith up until then on an open market, found that if the open market were to continue the farmer would probably be getting $1.50 a bushel for wheat. Therefore they stepped in, at long last, not to help the farmer, but because they realized that the open market was now going to work to the advantage of the farmer, whereas before it had worked to his disadvantage.
I want to remind the Minister of Trade and Commerce that about fifty-four per cent of the 1942 crop was sold by the farmers on the open market, and that they will get no benefit out of the participation certificates, or any increased price, for that wheat.
What is true of wheat was equally true of hogs. During the last two sessions hon. members on this side of the house tried to impress upon the Minister of Agriculture that, unless we got a price for hogs which was commensurate with the price of other commodities, and unless the farmers could have some help retained on their farms, they would be forced out of hog production. What happened? To bring the situation to a head, this fall a subsidy of ten cents a bushel on oats and fifteen cents a bushel on barley was paid. The farmers, short of help, now realized it was better to sell coarse grains than to use them for feed. Last fall the farmers began to go out of hogs; and what was most alarming to me, watching the figures, was that twenty to twenty-three per cent of the hogs being shipped were breeding hogs.

speechtext:
I am glad if I have succeeded in getting the minister on his feet. If I have got him. to break the veil of eilence I shall be more than satisfied.
When the farmers began to put their live stock on the market in such quantities that it was glutted1, the minister had to find a scapegoat, and the scapegoat he found was the C.I.O. workers in the packing plants whom he blamed for holding up the slaughtering of the farmers' hogs. I do not mind a man making a mistake,

and I do not mind, indeed I rather admire him if he accepts responsibility for it; but when he tries to lay the blame on a group of workers in the packing plants who are working long hours, often with inexperienced help, I think he is taking advantage of people who cannot answer back.
The objection which we have to the programme outlined by the government is that, while they may mention a social security measure here or a social security measure there, without any definite commitments, there is nothing to indicate that they propose to deal with the fundamental changes which must take place in our economy if we are to maintain full employment, provide a maximum market here in Canada, and provide for the exchange of our surplus commodities with other countries.
In the time allotted to me I cannot discuss the changes which must take place in other fields of our economy. I should like to say a few words about the changes which must take place in agriculture in order to enable it to pass from war-time economy into our peacetime economy with the minimum of dislocation for the country and. for the farmers. After all, we are on the threshold of a new era' as far as agriculture is concerned. As regards the decisions of the conference at Hot Springs, the united nations agreed to set up certain minimum nutritional standards whereby we shall guarantee to every man, woman and child in the united nations all the food they require, and guarantee to the farmers who produce that food an adequate living for doing so. If that policy is followed, then, as the vice-president of the United States has said, "the breath of the future is upon us," and we are now coming into a new era as far as agriculture is concerned.
I should like to outline here, briefly, twelve points, some of which we of this group have brought to the attention of the house before, and will continue to bring to the attention of the house throughout the session in asking the government to give these matters consideration. I enumerate them because I have no time to discuss them at length.
1.	The establishment of basic parity prices for all farm products; this price to bear a direct relationship to the cost of production. That is not a floor price, but a price which will vary with changing costs of production.
2.	The establishment of marketing boards for the purpose of carrying on orderly marketing of farm products.
We believe that, wherever two-thirds of the producers of any farm commodity agree, there should be set up a marketing board on which

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
there shall be adequate producer representation for the purpose of taking delivery of that particular product.
3.	A comprehensive system of crop insurance to apply to all Canadian farmers producing crops in which there is an element of risk.
The premiums for such crop insurance to be included when computing the basic parity price.
4.	The setting up of a board of live stock commissioners with power to license, regulate and control the facilities for assembling, transporting, yarding, slaughtering, processing and packing, together with the facilities for grading and selling all live stock and carcass products designed for human consumption, and in addition all live and dressed poultry and eggs should be subject to the jurisdiction of this board.
5.	The establishment of an agricultural bank for the refinancing of farm mortgages at a maximum rate of two and one-half per cent interest.
6.	The passing of a dominion cooperative act to enable farmers to establish cooperatives and to permit the coordination of present provincial cooperatives under a national charter.
7.	The setting up of a farm implement board for the purpose of working with the cooperatives in order to manufacture and distribute farm implements at the lowest possible cost.
8.	Federal and provincial legislation to provide that every farmer who is honestly endeavouring to pay his way Shall be able to retain his farm and to pass it on unencumbered to his children or to make such other disposition of it as he may see fit.
9.	The establishment of an ever-normal granary to store surpluses of non-perishable goods, and the building of storage facilities in order to carry a reserve of prepared and processed goods which are of a perishable nature.
10.	The setting up of export and import boards in order to dispose of surplus products in conformity with the principle laid down by the united nations conference on food and agriculture held at Hot Springs, Virginia, last May, at which it was agreed that freedom from want of food suitable and adequate for the health and strength of our people can be achieved and that in supplying this food the producers can and should be adequately rewarded.
11.	The provision of large sums for soil and water conservation and for irrigation projects in order to preserve Canada's farm lands and to provide employment in the post-war period.
12.	Immediate research into the field of chemurgy. The erection of factories in western Canada after the war for the purpose of utilizing agricultural products for industrial purposes.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that this would constitute a bold and imaginative programme for agriculture. We believe that unless we are prepared to adopt such a programme we shall not lay the economic base without which it is impossible to have in this country either full employment or adequate social security.

I had not intended 'to speak
in this debate, but in view of the challenge which the last speaker (Mr. Douglas, Wey-burn) has given I shall say a few things with reference to what he has stated to the house.
In the first place he has suggested that no minister during this debate, excepting the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), has spoken up to the present time, and he has been more or less critical of that fact. Well, at the beginning of the debate I had understood that it was the consensus of the house generally that we should do everything possible to shorten the debate. Members of the government have a number of opportunities upon which to deal with the questions with which their departments are particularly concerned. When estimates are brought before the house it is our opportunity to place upon Hansard a record of all the activities of the different departments, and we have the opportunities which are presented when we are bringing down legislation. We have also the opportunities which are presented when members from different parts of the house ask questions on the orders of the day, and I took advantage to-day of one such question in order to place certain information before *the house.
The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne has never been regarded as the special opportunity for ministers of the crown. Rather it has been looked upon as the special opportunity of private members to voice their views, a time when they have the privilege of speaking on any question concerning matters of government. I think therefore that ministers are to be commended rather than condemned if, on an occasion of this kind when it has been considered essential by all that the debate should be shortened as much as possible, they allow private members to take up the greater part if not the whole of the time devoted to debate.
Wrhen the hon. member for Weyburn rose he said he would agree with a statement made by
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

the leader of the house, the Prime Minister, and on this occasion I would like to agree with the statement made by his leader the other night, when, as I noticed, the hon. member for Weyburn was not as much in agreement with what that hon. gentleman said as I was, judging from the expression on his face. When the Prime Minister was discussing these matters the other day he referred to a number of things, one of which was the advisability of appealing to the people at the end of a term of office; and that has been referred to by the hon. member for Weyburn. Another matter touched upon was the advisability of leaders of parties, who intend to represent the people, finding a seat in the house where it is meant that they should attend to lead their group. I was surprised to hear my hon. friend, referring to that matter a few moments ago, say that the present government in Saskatchewan has not called an election, in constituencies which have been vacated within the last few months, in order to make it possible for him to enter the house in that province.
It has been, I believe, the almost invariable custom for members of a party who already have seats in the house to resign a seat and challenge the government to put up a candidate against their leader when he has been chosen to lead them in the house. But in the province of Saskatchewan, where by the way the real leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party is serving his country overseas with the armies of the empire, a convention was called during that gentleman's absence and a new leader was chosen. That new leader holds a seat in this house, and I am not surprised that no follower of the real leader of the C.C.F. party, who is at present serving overseas, has seen fit to resign his seat in the house in Saskatchewan in order to make it possible for the hon. member to contest that constituency.
What gave me considerable pleasure, when listening to the hon. member for Weyburn say that he agreed with statements made by my leader, was the privilege which I have of agreeing with statements made by his leader,-

The next point that occurs to me is one that was brought up by his leader the other day. It seems to be a favorite topic of discussion when C.C.F. speakers make speeches, either in this house or outside, to refer to the Liberal platform of 1919. He brings into the house a copy of an old paper and recites that platform. He reads it to the house and makes no explanations with regard to it and then he proceeds to be critical. I had the privilege of being on the resolutions committee of the convention of 1919 as representative of the Liberal group who were sitting in the legislature of Saskatchewan at that time, and I would like to tell members of this house, including the leader of the C.C.F. party and his chief supporter, the leader of the C.C.F. party in the province of Saskatchewan, that that convention was made up of representation from the Liberal parties from every province in the dominion and from the different sections of the different provinces which had more than one Liberal organization represented. The information submitted to the resolutions committee and to the convention as a whole was a document about three-quarters of an inch thick and it contained the plaftorms of all the Liberal parties in all the provinces of Canada. Those platforms were studied, and out of them, with the assistance of men representing every provincial Liberal group in Canada, there was worked the platform from which my hon. friend was reading.
What has happened since that time? The Liberals went back to the provinces. They did not do what my hon. friend has done here to-day-suggest that the government of Canada should start to direct the activities of the provinces. They went back to the provinces and in their own legislatures they placed upon the statute books of those provinces the legislation that was embodied in the principles of Liberalism as drawn by the 1919 convention in so far as they related to provincial affairs. My hon. friend comes here this afternoon and instead of reciting these facts he starts to read twelve points drafted in Regina a short time ago-at a meeting behind closed doors, by the way-that ought

It has clinics which have been operating for many years. It has maternity grants, mothers' allowances, et cetera. I could go on and recite one social service after another. Does anyone suggest we are going to bring legislation into this house without consulting the provinces that have these services established, in order to determine what the relationship is to be in the future between the set-up of this government to administer such legislation and the set-up that already exists in the provinces? Of course the thing is unthinkable. But the point I wish to make is this, that the platform of 1919 recommended that all these things enunciated as policies of the Liberal party be brought into effect by any institution of government that we might have in the dominion, from the municipalities up to the parliament-which meets in Ottawa, and much of it has been brought into effect.

speechtext:
I am coming to that, too, in a moment. My hon. friend (Mr. Wright) has asked about sows, and because he is a farmer, and differs in that respect from the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), he will understand what I am going to say. My hon, friend knows that when you are marketing 33 1/3 per cent more hogs on the market you are going to market more sows on the market, too.
When did these farmers decide to market their sows? It was not after changes were made in the Canadian prices of feed grain in September. It was not after an announcement of policy on October 22. They had started to do it away back in June, and, so far as these figures are concerned, they carried it right through July, August and September, into October, and right down to the time we put the embargo on, about which the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has been talking. And then the marketing of sows went down, naturally.
Why were they up before? The hon. jnember for Melfort knows that many other farmers did what I did. Those of us in western Canada who raise hogs know this, that unless you have a superior kind of equipment you cannot raise successfully and market more than one litter of hogs, especially in
[Mr. Gardiner.)
Saskatchewan, from any one sow in any one year. What we do when we undertake to increase our production is this, if we are doing the thing we ought to do: We take a gilt that was littered, let us say in April or March, and we breed that sow in December of that year or January of the following year. Thus we have pigs from her when she is a year old. We wean the pigs in May or June. Then we sell the sow. Naturally anyone who is carrying on business on his farm economically in the western provinces marketed his sows as early as he could. And those of us who did not get them marketed before the embargo was put on found ourselves with sows on our hands. Yes, we found ourselves with those sows on our hands. That is no indication there was or was not to be a reduction in hog production. It is an indication that we just missed. We should have sold our sows, and would have been better off if we had done it. These high sales of sows in Canada during that period were natural to greatly increased production. It was good business for the farmers to sell their sows during that time.
My hon. friend says we have come to the time when the production of hogs in Canada is down. I gave figures earlier this afternoon indicating that if we market the number of pigs that we have been marketing for the last three months we shall have close to a billion pounds of bacon to send to Great Britain this year, even with increased marketings of hogs in Canada at the present time. I notice my hon. friend shakes his head. Well, he shook his head a year ago when I said that. He shook his head two years ago when I said it. They have been shaking their heads for four years. In other words, I agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) when he says that the people of Canada are not going to believe in people who make mistakes so often. The production of hogs has been going up every year, and it is still going up. Our problem to-day is not the problem of getting greater production in order to supply the market that we have. Our problem is to get shipping in order to take the hogs from where they have been produced, to the British market, or from where they are to some other part of the Canadian market. That is our problem to-day. And that is so with nearly all the farm products we have been discussing in the house.
May I say that no member of the British government since this war started has ever suggested to the government of Canada that we are not measuring up to our obligations in connection with the production of hogs. As a matter of fact, my colleague who sits in front of me went to Great Britain in the fall of

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
1939; and with the best efforts and support he could get from the officials of my department he was able to make a contract in Great Britain for only 291,000,000 pounds of bacon and ham. It was not until well on in that season that they consented to take 330,000,000 pounds, the amount we had for sale.
I myself went to Great Britain in October of 1940, and I worked on a contract. I tried to persuade the British that they needed the 425,000,000 pounds of bacon we had in sight at that time. After I had been there a month I came back to this house. What was the criticism I heard? The criticism was that I had been dickering with the British government and refusing to accept the price they were able to pay, in spite of the fact that we had these great quantities of bacon products to sell. But inside of two or three months, when my friends got out into the country, what did we hear? The story then was that we had not foreseen what did happen, and that we should have taken proper action to serve a greater market. When the time came we had the quantity available. Then my friends said, "You will not have enough." In 1942 we had 600,000,000 pounds; in 1943 we had 675,000,000, -and this year they are coming in faster than they have ever come in in any preceding years. Our concern to-day is this: What are we going to do with them? That concern requires us to make some changes, and to evolve policies to take care of the matter. In working out these policies we must of necessity. communicate with our friends to the south. Why? Before our American friends came into the war we stopped Shipment of our food from this country, to the extent that was required, in order that we might send more to Great Britain. Since the Americans came into the war they have been lease-lending food to Great Britain, and much of that food is the same kind of food we produce in Canada. Through an understanding which we have with them we attempt to lend-lease our own food to Great Britain, and they lend-lease theirs. Producing all the food we possibly can for our own consumption and for British consumption, we have found the desire to produce to the limit on both sides of the line to have resulted in our packing plants being filled to capacity with hogs, with cattle, and with meat products of all kinds. The shipping from both countries is not sufficient to take care of our meat supplies, for all concerned. Some adjustments have to be made. But these adjustments are made by the shipping board, which has a very strong representation on it from the British government. As they require these greater quantities of food, from time to time,
they will see to it that the ships get here to take it away, and in that way we will find a market for it.
But in the meantime there are certain things which have to be considered in connection with that matter. We shall have to be a little bit patient about some matters, and not simply say that because yesterday we did not have the market open into the United States and something 'has happened here that creates difficulty for us, at a time when there are just as great difficulties on the other side of the line, we should take off our restrictions and throw the food to them so that they will have trouble with it. That cannot be done in war time, when we have problems which concern us both.
Our intention is to get as much as possible of this meat over to the British front, where it is required, and to the fronts where our soldiers are fighting in different parts of the world. But what I wish to emphasize is the fact that our friends are still doing what they have been doing ever since this war started:	They
are praying for a calamity to come, and it has never come in so far as agricultural production is concerned. They are not quite big enough-
I am not a big man myself-to stand up in their places and say that in spite of their prophecies last year, in spite of their prophecies of the year before, and in spite of their prophecies of the year before that, agriculture in Canada has gone on to greater and greater heights in production, and has done that in spite of the fact-this is their next statement on most occasions-that our opponents claim we have had a muddling of man-power in this country. When my hon. friend gets up and says, "You have not enough labour in agriculture, you have not enough labour in industry, you have not enough labour in shipping, you have not enough labour in our transportation organizations, you have not enough labour in our schools to teach our children, you have not enough labour in our armed forces," what does that mean? That means that all the available man-power of this country is engaged in prosecuting this war. That is all it means.
With reduced man-power upon the farm we have produced forty^eight per cent more farm products than we produced in the last year before the war. That does not indicate any muddling in man-power; it indicates that the man-power of this country is working more effectively and to better purpose than ever before. Why? An hon. member, I think it was the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), said last night that I said something the other day about the necessity of having markets for our products. He made light of that statement. He lost the point entirely of
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

what I saidi. In the speech from which he was quoting I stated that in spite of the fact that we have reduced the man-power and woman-power on our farms by almost half a million we were producing over forty per cent more tonnage of food than we produced in the last year before the war. I went on to say that in spite of the fact that we have purchasing power in Canada greater in proportion to our population than we have ever had before, we are able to eat only six per cent more food in tonnage than we ate before the war. When those two facts are considered, I am afraid that those who criticize the statement that we must export some of it from this country, in other words find a market elsewhere for it, are advocates of the policy they sometimes accuse us of advocating, namely, a policy of scarcity, producing less so that you can sell each unit at a higher price. That would be the only policy which would be an alternative to the one I suggested in the remarks I have just made. That would be applicable to all primary production as well as other products produced from the natural resources of this country with the labour of Canadian people.
If my hon. friend really wants to know what the Liberal policy is, let me tell him that the whole intent of Liberal policy has been the same since it was first laid down in principle by economists and political leaders in the British isles. I said the same thing before the war; I said it again during the war, and I think it ought to be taken as proof that I should say it again after the war is over. If a man is right once, he ought to repeat the thing; if he is right the second time, he ought to say it again and not dio as my hon. friends do, express one statement in the fall of 1939 with regard to the war and possible production, and then change that statement in 1942, make a new guess, and then change it in 1943 and make another guess. Then when we are in the fifth year of the war we find that they are still going right on guessing.
We on this side of the house are convinced that there is only one thing for the people of Canada to do in order to provide the amount of employment we talk about, and that is to produce everything that we are constituted to produce in the greatest possible quantity and then look about the world for places which produce the things we would like to have and without which we cannot live at the standard at which we desire to live, and endeavour to trade our surpluses with them. Someone said the other day that we had been twenty-five years in bringing that policy into effect. May I say to the hon. member who said that that in 1932 we got down to the lowest level of trade in relation to production in this country.

There was a slight come-back down to 1934. What did we say to the people in 1935? We said that if we were put in power we would go out through the world where people are disunited and discontented and endeavour to make trade agreements. We made something over twenty and in spite of the threat of war we increased our trade with the outside world by fifty per cent. While increasing that trade by fifty per cent we decreased unemployment by fifty per cent. That is an indication of what the policy will do under the most difficult possible conditions in peace time.
What do my hon. friends say? They say, "No; give us socialism." Where did they go to find it, They went to the only countries where there was national socialism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I was stating when I was interrupted was that there was a reason why young men in those countries were not riding the rods. Those of us who belong to the Liberal party, and perhaps some others, gave that as a reason at the time. One of the reasons why I myself gave it in the years following 1936 was that I had the privilege of sitting in the gallery of the House of Commons in London in 1936, and I listened to the man who was sitting on the right-hand corner, as I faced him, in the front bench just across from the government. He

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
was asking the government of Great Britain of that time, which I have heard my friends condemn on quite a number of occasions, for the privilege of forming a small committee, a committee of four or five members of the house, and of meeting the government in council in order to discuss the conditions existing over on the continent of Europe which made unemployment not a possibility there at that time. After he had stated his case, a member of the government rose and denied him that right, and said that no member of the house knew better than he did that any hon. member could go to the government at any time and discuss any subject as important as that with the government, but they did not consider that any small group in the house knew so much more than the government itself knew with regard to that situation to lend sufficient importance to it to have a meeting of that kind. Well, now, that was during a debate on defence, and what he was trying to point out was that they were building on -the continent of Europe at that time the greatest war machine the world has ever seen. At that time the man who was giving that warning got a very indifferent hearing, both in the house and outside. War came, and during the period before the war there was unemployment for reasons I have been indicating, namely, that we could not sell our products in the countries that were preparing for war against us. The war came in 1939, and it had been in progress only a few months when that same man was called to the premiership of Great Britain, and he has led us through the war. And what have we found out during that period? We have found that we could end unemployment by building a war machine. The United States has found the same thing; Britain has found the same thing; every country in the world has found the same thing; and in building a war machine at least as great as -that of our opponents we have for the time being brought about lack of unemployment in -the country. But, like my hon. friend who spoke last night, I am not going to follow the socialists into the next election or into the future and maintain that, in order to end unemployment, we must have the same kind of regimentation and control throughout peace time as was required in those various countries for war whether in preparation for or during war.
What is needed in the world is the new spirit spoken of by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and ridiculed a few moments ago by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). My hon. friend apparently does not understand what the brotherhood of man
leads to. The brotherhood of man does not lead to nationalism, with consumption in your own country of everything you are going to produce, and only^the production of those things which you can consume in your own country. The spirit of the brotherhood of man leads to the production of all -that can be produced in this country of those things which -are needed in other parts of the world, and the distribution -of them to all parts of the world. That is the ideal of Liberalism and it has been the ideal of Liberalism ever since the Liberal party has been known in Canada.
One thing that pleases me is that most other parties in this country are coming to think the same thing, and when they do come to think the same and meet behind closed doors in Winnipeg or Regina to draft a new platform, what do they do? A new platform in these days toward the end or in the middle of the war, days during which we are fighting for the freedoms that Liberalism has established in different countries throughout the world, under whatever name the principle may have operated, means simply this, that these people take up all the things done by the Liberal party, provincially and federally, and recite them as their own.
My hon. friends opposite say that floor prices came from John Bracken. They forget that we had a floor price under butter in 1938. They forget that we had a floor price under hogs and cheese in 1939-40. They forget that we had a floor price-their own party put a floor price, if you like to go back-of 87i cents under wheat when Mr. Bennett was in power, but they have dropped the name of his party. We have put floor prices all the way from 70 cents to $1.25 under wheat at different times, and if anyone cares to search the records he will find that the week before Mr. Bracken made the announcement of his policies in Lethbridge I announced this particular policy, in connection with floor prices, in London on October 15 last, and the Prime Minister himself read it over the radio- into the platform of this party very shortly after. The Prime Minister tells me that it was in the platform of the Federation before Mr. Bracken spoke.
In any event, a floor under farm products has been the policy of this government ever since the war started1, and all we have said in any policy announced lately is that we shall bring down legislation to make it possible for us to apply that policy when the war ends to those products to which at present we can apply it, under the War Measures Act. The War Measures Act, as it now stands, applies only for six months after the war. We are to bring down legislation which will make it
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

possible for us to have floors under farm prices put into effect by this government and maintained beyond the war.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) raised the constitutional question the other night, and someone else said that floors may be in the basement, while still another person said something else about it. Well, I should say this. My hon. friends opposite ask, where will you find markets? I have been saying something about that in the last few moments; but the market that has always been supplied, where floor prices have been involved, is the market supplied by the government of this country when it says that when products reach a certain price we shall take control of them and then try to find a market for them, after having taken them over at that price. There is nothing constitutionally wrong with that. There may be some other things that are difficult about it, but constitutionally there is nothing wrong with it.
And so finally, with regard to the attack made this afternoon, I say that we have in Canada an agricultural policy of which we are proud. We have the satisfaction of being able to stand anywhere in the dominion and say that the returns from agricultural products are better than they ever were previously in the whole history of the country, war time or any other time. We have the further satisfaction of being able to say that men are getting out of the debts they incurred during times when some others were administering the affairs of this country, that men are paying their debts and getting into the position where they can go on at the end of the war and operate more successfully than ever before.
My hon. friend makes an appeal to us to help those who are coming back from overseas. I agree with the hon. member who spoke from over in the corner the other day, after returning from overseas, that to be able to say that you are doing more than any other country has done is not enough. I do say, however, that we are doing so much and attempting to do so much more that I am quite sure that what another returned man said the other night over the radio is true, namely, that if the young men over there knew all the things he knows, after listening to certain things he has heard since coming here, they would be fairly well satisfied with what the Canadian government is doing to prepare for their home-coming. And those things which we have not done and which probably have not occurred to us, those things which others are suggesting ought to be done, are always given full consideration, and if they are helpful they are adopted from time to time as, I have no doubt, they will be adopted in the future.

This government is in every sense a liberal government and we do not intend to apply state socialism either to agriculture or to any other line of industry in order to bring about prosperity in Canada, because we know that in a free world such as we shall have after the war, where there will not be national socialist states in Europe, where people will be prepared to trade with one another, and to trea't one another as brother men, conditions will be very much better under a spirit of Liberalism than under any other spirit which can be established in this country.

Mr. Speaker, in support of my argument I should like to refer to the January issue of "Canada at War". I find on'examining this booklet that thirty-five per cent of the man-power of Canada between the ages of eighteen and forty-five has joined the armed services. The sixty-five per cent at home includes cripples and many who have tried unsuccessfully to join the services. They, with women, children and the old people, have done a remarkable job for which the government of this country should not take too much credit. This job has been done in spite of the feeling in agriculture that the farmers are the forgotten people, in spite of the feeling amongst labour that the workers of this country are not accorded the consideration that the employers are receiving. Notwithstanding that, I find on page 39 of this publication that the production of miscellaneous military stores in 1943 was nearly six times as much as in 1939 and 1940, mechanical transport four times as much, cargo and naval vessels twenty times as much, aircraft eight times as much, armoured vessels ten times as much, guns and small arms 196 tipies as much, guns and ammunition fourteen times as much, instruments and signalling apparatus sixty-one times as much, chemicals seventy-six times as much, small arms thirty-seven times as much. In the field of agriculture our farmers have a wonderful record. In 1943 we had on the farms only three farmers for every four we had in 1939, but per farmer in Canada as a whole twice as much was produced. In connection with our shipments of pork products to the United Kingdom in 1943, this booklet shows that they were about three hundred per cent of what we sent in 1939. about fifty per cent more of wheat, about two hundred per cent more canned fish, about fifty per cent more cheese and about forty times as many eggs.
I should like to correct the impression that the minister gave that we were consuming only six per cent more food in 1943 than in 1935-39. In this publication I find that we were consuming 18 per cent more dairy products than we consumed in the 1935-39 period, 12 per cent more meats. We were up to 29 per cent in beef; poultry, 2 per cent; eggs, 24 per cent; potatoes, 7 per cent; tomatoes and citrus fruits, 20 per cent; coffee, 11 per cent, and cocoa, 19 per cent. In a few items we were down: tea, refined sugar and butter.
