speechtext:
Yes, and the white men must take responsibility for bringing this plague to the first citizens of Canada. Having brought it to them, we must see to it that these fine citizens have the sort of treatment they deserve.
I should like now to discuss the question of health services in connection with those in our mental institutions. The deputy minister of health of Ontario gave evidence before the committee last year to the effect that 17,000 more beds were required to meet the situation in Canada. Doctor Heagerty said we had
47.000	patients in our mental institutions and that we were short about 10,000 beds to accommodate them. He al$o said there were not enough doctors or nurses or orderlies to care for the patients properly; and he pointed out that we have been told by experts that a
great deal of mental illness is preventable. Specialists tell us that if they could get hold of children who have either the hereditary factor or an inclination toward mental illness they could do away with a great deal of it.
Coming to the question of our general health services, I have obtained a great deal of information from the bureau of statistics in regard to our provision for the health of the people of this country. I find that according to the 1941 census we had a doctor for every 1,098 people in the dominion. The figures for 1941 by provinces for doctors and dentists, not including those in the armed forces, are as follows:
	Persons	Persons

Canada 	1,098	3,121Prince Edwrard Island	1.419	4,320Nova Scotia 	1,350	3.959New Brunswick 	1,694	4,529Quebec	1,107	3,883Ontario	927	2,318Manitoba 	1,107	3,475Saskatchewan 	1,700	4,766Alberta 	1,320	3.961British Columbia ....	1,010	2.548
These statistics prove clearly that people in all parts of Canada are not given the advantage of adequate medical service. In my own riding we have eleven doctors practising now, each looking after an average of 5,217 people. Our three practising dentists look after an average of 19,131 each. I am informed1 that in the Canadian army we have a doctor to care for every 245 soldiers, a dentist to look after every 535, and a nurse for every 294. In the army, of course, provision must be made to look after the wounded, after they have joined in battle. But I cannot see any reason why it is necessary to have a dentist for every 535 in the Canadian army, and why the people in the Mackenzie riding should have to get along with a dentist for every 19,131 people.
Before the war we were not in quite such a serious situation. We had a dentist for every
11,000	people. I wonder if hon. members realize what it means to people in different parts of the country who have to live year after year without being able to go to a hospital or a doctor? In 1930 I found my abode at Hudson Bay Junction, in the north country. We had left Edinburgh, Scotland, where the very best of medical services were available for every man, woman and child. The Scottish, people are much maligned, but it should be said for them-

speechtext:
Too many. In the city of Edinburgh is found one of the finest hospitals in the old country, the Royal infirmary. There
The Address-Mr. Nicholson

one receives the very best of treatment, and a bill is never submitted. The Hudson Bay Junction district was served by one medical doctor who cared for farmers, townsfolk and about 800 men working in the bush. But when the depression came, and the sawmill operators could not sell their lumber, many of the mills closed down.
At the same time, large numbers of people in the drought area came north, and brought with them very little money. I happen to have with me the pictures of three of the heroes of the last war, who came north from the city of Regina. In one case the man is fighting for democracy for the second time. The two others have sons fighting in this war. The arrangement was made whereby they would receive $10 a month for food, for the first year, and that they would have other expenses which would not make a total expenditure of more than $300 for the year. It does not require much imagination to appreciate that the $10 a month to city dwellers going to the north would not allow much for medical services. It would be used for the purchase of foodstuffs.
Accordingly the board of trade and the citizens in the community thought something should be done by the government of the day to provide medical servicq for these settlers. They were being given food, and it was argued that medical service was also important. What I am about to say is for the benefit of my hon. friends to the right, the Progressive Conservatives. While many of them would rather not take responsibility for the administration of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, as he was then known-now Viscount Bennett-and for the Conservative administration in the province, I must remind the house that many of those who are now supporting the Progressive Conservative party were active in the Conservative party at that time.
What did the government of the province say? It said, "This is a matter the people must look after themselves." vNo help was provided. Conservatives said, "Our doctor is a Liberal ; if he were not such an, active Liberal the administration might do something about it." Liberals said, "If we had a Liberal government a different policy would be carried out."

speechtext:
Doctor Collins, who
practised in Hudson Bay Junction at that 
time. By and by we did have a change of government. Under that Liberal administration we did get much better treatment.- We were without a doctor for some considerable time, as no doctor could provide medical service for this large area under such conditions. There was not a doctor within seventy miles when he left for another location. His going was a great loss to our community.
How would hon. members like to live in a community where there was no doctor within seventy miles to look after people who became sick. But when the Liberal government did decide to do something about those people, they madte provision for $50 a month to pay the doctor. The doctor had to agree that every person who was on relief could come to him and receive treatment. He was not prevented from making additional collections. But people who were getting $10 a month for relief, and were selling cordwood at a dollar a cord were not likely to be able to pay much to a medical doctor. However, the doctor was concerned about the health of the people, and he did accept $50 a month from the provincial government, and did give medical service to the people in a very large area.
I submit that $50 a month to give comprehensive service to such a large number of people in an area where the nearest hospital and doctor is seventy miles away is not sufficient. Many of the people in that area were men who had fought for their king and country at the time of the last war. That was one of the areas which was available for settlement when they came back from overseas. They settled on these bush homesteads, up in the north country.
After criticizing ourselves for our failure to care for people in times of sickness, we might ask ourselves if people in other countries have done better. If we examine the evidence placed before us in this large volume by the advisory committee I think we shall find that there are two countries which have outstanding records, as far as providing health for their citizens is concerned. I refer to New Zealand and Russia. And, in passing, I urge hon. members to take advantage of the opportunity to hear Doctor Sigerist this evening in the Glebe collegiate, or to-morrow before he leaves the city. Hear what this outstanding professor of the history of medicine has to say about what has been done in Russia.
In his book, which I have before me, I find
some significant statements. He says this:
It seems to me that the following four points represent the mdst characteristic features of the soviet health system:
1.	Medical service is free and therefore available to all;

The Address-Mr. Nicholson
2.	The prevention of disease is in the foreground of all health activities;
3.	All health activities are directed by central bodies, the people's commissariats of health, with the result that-
4.	Health can be planned on a large scale.
Then he says:
There can be no doubt that the soviet system of social insurance is infinitely superior to any insurance system in capitalist countries. The costs are what they should be, part of the cost of production. The benefits are infinitely greater than under any other insurance scheme. The worker is guaranteed complete medical service, he is given social security. He is entitled to it, because after all, he is creating the values that make such a scheme possible.
Most people are agreed that changes will have to be made in our health programme in Canada. Some doubts exist as to what type of changes should be made. I have here a copy of "You Knew What You Were Voting For", written by William S. Gibson, President of National Cellulose of Canada, Limited.
On page eight he says:
All the planners start with the premise- "We must not have another depression." I could bring many arguments to show that nations and individuals profit more in adversity than in good times. I know that I would rather start a new enterprise during a depression than in good times.
Of course Mr. Gibson would rather start an enterprise in poor times. In January I talked to a man working in one of the sawmills in my riding. He is receiving forty cents an hour and his board, but he told me that the first time he met me, in 1932 or 1933, he was working for four cents an hour for a ten-hour day. They could not even make it five cents an hour. Naturally Mr. Gibson would rather start an industry when he could have his materials produced by men working in the bush for four cents an hour, when there are fifty men looking for every job available.
I think this war has proven one thing conclusively. It has proven that if we want it we can have a high standard of living in Canada in the world of to-morrow. We should understand that a nation can plan its production and consumption on a low plane, with mass unemployment and low standards, or on a high plane with full employment and high standards for its people. I should like to point out that it was stated by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), when he was Minister of Finance, that whatever is physically possible must be made financially possible. His successor, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), has emphasized that. We must always keep that in mind. If that is true in war time, then it is equally true in peace time. Whatever is physically possible in peace time must be financially possible.
I have not the time to go into all the details that must be considered, but finance is not now and should not be a limiting factor in our effort in any direction. The only limiting factors should be: first, raw materials; second, labour; third, the machinery of pn>
duction and, fourth, our power to coordinate these things. I submit that if the war should end to-morrow-we know that victory will be achieved some day-Canada would be a richer nation than ever before. By that I mean that we would have more new factories, more trained workers and more new resources to develop.
In order to plan a health programme for the post-war period there are certain physical necessities which must be kept in mind. We must have: first, nutritious food; second, adequate supplies of heat, light, potable water, sewage disposal facilities and fresh air; third, preventive and restrictive health services; fourth, adequate clothing and proper housing for all our citizens. I shall have something to say about most of these at some future time.
Mention was made a few days ago by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) of an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal and which had been prompted by the report of a speech by Mr. Jolliffe, leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Ontario. During a discussion before a group of eminent medical men Mr. Jolliffe outlined in some detail the plans of the C.C.F. for improved medical services. This was during a meeting of the London academy of medicine on September 23, 1943. In his remarks Mr. Jolliffe made it quite clear that on the whole the doctors of this country had done a good job. We do not want to place the doctors of Canada in a position where they are not going to have a great deal of freedom. The president of the Canadian medical association made some reference to the fact that the C.CE. would limit the salaries of general practitioners to $3,000, and of specialists to $8,000. I have made a careful survey and I can find no record anywhere where any C.C.F. speaker made any statement of that kind.
I would remind the house that in Russia they have provided the highest standard of living available for their doctors. The C.C.F. in any province in Canada would recognize that our doctors are highly trained and must be given as high a standard of living as we can provide collectively.
Then the hon. member for Peterborough West asked if the C.C.F. could arrange for babies to be delivered between eight a.m. and five p.m., but no answer was given. Both the editorial in the Journal and the hon. member for Peterborough West assume that

Post-War Reconstruction
no answer could be given. Again I would remind the house that arrangements have been made to look after the medical and dental needs of our troops without any one doctor having to work for twenty-four hours a day.
Some of my best friends are of the medical profession and I have the greatest respect for them, but there is one thing I must say about them. While they are ready to look after their friends, most of them seem to be unable to look after themselves. Many of them are burnt out by the time they reach fifty or fifty-five years. We must provide machinery so that the medical services of this country can be carried on without any one doctor having to work for sixteen or twenty hours a day.
On motion of Mr. Marshall the debate was adjourned.
